newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka takes peace package to war-torn north.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka takes peace package to war-torn north.

text.p: Thousands of Tamil civilians in the war-torn north of Sri Lanka have been attending meetings to listen to officials explain devolution proposals aimed at ending the country's ethnic war, a government minister said on Thursday.

The meetings -- the first to be held in the northern Jaffna peninsula, a former Tamil Tiger stronghold -- were part of a campaign launched by the government to win support from minority Tamils for the proposals, Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Gamini Peiris said.
Jaffna was captured by the army last year. Since then thousands of people who fled the area because of the government's war with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) have returned.

"An open dialogue was encouraged and the participants were invited to raise questions and concerns regarding the constitutional reforms process with particular reference to the devolution of power," Peiris told a news conference.

The government has proposed a new constitution that includes devolution of powers to administrative units in a bid to partly meet the LTTE's demand for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east.

Peiris said government officials and a group of Sinhala and Tamil intellectuals had recently held 19 meetings in Jaffna. More than 4,000 people had attended the meetings and a majority expressed strong support for the proposals, he said.
Sinhalese are the major ethnic group in Sri Lanka.
The reforms are currently bogged in a parliamentary select committee where President Chandrika Kumaratunga's ruling People's Alliance is battling opposition parties for a consensus.

Last month, Kumaratunga told a two-day meeting of her lawmakers that she could be forced to hold a non-binding national referendum on the proposals ahead of taking them to parliament if the opposition's support was not forthcoming.
Kumaratunga is scheduled to launch a campaign in late August to address meetings across the country to explain the proposals.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the ethnic war, now in its 15th year. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
